nodes.statement: An (undirected) graph is a pair G = (V,E) consisting of a set V and a multi-set E of unordered pairs of elements in V. Elements of V are called vertices and elements of E are called edges. For two vertices u,v in V, we say u and v are adjacent if \u,v\ in E. We call an undirected graph G simple if all edges are distinct (i.e., E is a set), and each edge is a pair of distinct vertices.
nodes.raw_latex:
An \textit{(undirected) graph} is a pair $G = (V,E)$ consisting of a set $V$ 
  and a multi-set $E$ of unordered pairs of elements in $V$. 
  Elements of $V$ are called \textit{vertices} and elements of $E$ are called \textit{edges}.
  For two vertices $u,v \in V$, we say $u$ and $v$ are \textit{adjacent} if $\{u,v\} \in E$.
  We call an undirected graph $G$ \textit{simple} if all edges are distinct (i.e., $E$ is a set), 
  and each edge is a pair of distinct vertices.
nodes.clean_text: An (undirected) graph is a pair G = (V,E) consisting of a set V and a multi-set E of unordered pairs of elements in V. Elements of V are called vertices and elements of E are called edges. For two vertices u,v in V, we say u and v are adjacent if \u,v\ in E. We call an undirected graph G simple if all edges are distinct (i.e., E is a set), and each edge is a pair of distinct vertices.

nodes.statement: A directed graph is a pair G = (V,E) consisting of a set V and a multi-set E of ordered pairs of elements in V. Elements of V are called vertices and elements of E are called edges. We call a directed graph G simple if all edges are distinct and each edge is a pair of distinct vertices.
nodes.raw_latex:
A \textit{directed graph} is a pair $G = (V,E)$ consisting of a set $V$ 
  and a multi-set $E$ of ordered pairs of elements in $V$. 
  Elements of $V$ are called \textit{vertices} and elements of $E$ are called \textit{edges}.
  We call a directed graph $G$ \textit{simple} if all edges are distinct and
  each edge is a pair of distinct vertices.

We call a directed graph G simple if all edges are distinct and each edge is a pair of distinct vertices.

nodes.name: Reachability
nodes.statement: Let G be a simple graph or a simple directed graph. A vertex v is reachable from u if some walk realized in G runs from u to v. In the undirected case reachability is an equivalence relation on VG; in the directed case it is only a preorder, since walks cannot be reversed.
nodes.clean_text: Let G be a simple graph or a simple directed graph. A vertex v is reachable from u if some walk realized in G runs from u to v. In the undirected case reachability is an equivalence relation on VG; in the directed case it is only a preorder, since walks cannot be reversed.
nodes.label: def:reachable-directed

nodes.name: Symmetric orientation
nodes.statement: The symmetric orientation of a simple graph G is the simple directed graph on VG whose arcs are the ordered pairs (u, v) with \u, v\ in EG. A walk is realized in G exactly when it is realized in the symmetric orientation, so reachability and distances agree.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:symmetric-orientation}
  
  
  The \emph{symmetric orientation} of a simple graph $G$ is the simple directed graph on
  $\V{G}$ whose arcs are the ordered pairs $(u, v)$ with $\{u, v\} \in \E{G}$. A walk is
  realized in $G$ exactly when it is realized in the symmetric orientation, so
  reachability and distances agree.
nodes.clean_text: The symmetric orientation of a simple graph G is the simple directed graph on VG whose arcs are the ordered pairs (u, v) with \u, v\ in EG. A walk is realized in G exactly when it is realized in the symmetric orientation, so reachability and distances agree.
nodes.label: def:symmetric-orientation

nodes.name: Distance
nodes.statement: The distance dist(u, v) in N cup \infty\ from u to v in a simple directed graph is the least length of a walk from u to v, and infty if v is not reachable from u. For a simple graph it is the distance in the symmetric orientation, and is then symmetric in u and v.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:dist}
  
  
  
  The \emph{distance} $\dist(u, v) \in \N \cup \{\infty\}$ from $u$ to $v$ in a simple
  directed graph is the least length of a walk from $u$ to $v$, and $\infty$ if $v$ is not
  reachable from $u$. For a simple graph it is the distance in the symmetric orientation,
  and is then symmetric in $u$ and $v$.
nodes.clean_text: The distance dist(u, v) in N cup \infty\ from u to v in a simple directed graph is the least length of a walk from u to v, and infty if v is not reachable from u. For a simple graph it is the distance in the symmetric orientation, and is then symmetric in u and v.
nodes.label: def:dist

nodes.name: BFS layers
nodes.statement: Let s in VG. The layers of breadth-first search from s are the sets \[ L_0 = \s\, L_k+1 = N^+(L_k) setminus (L_0 cup dots cup L_k), \] where N^+(L) denotes the set of out-neighbours of the vertices of L. The set of vertices visited within k rounds is V_k = L_0 cup dots cup L_k. When s notin VG every layer is empty. In Lean the search is a state (V_k, L_k) iterated k times from (\s\, \s\), so that the definition reduces and decide can evaluate it.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{def:bfs-layers}
  
  
  Let $s \in \V{G}$. The \emph{layers} of breadth-first search from $s$ are the sets
  \[
    L_0 = \{s\}, \qquad
    L_{k+1} = N^+(L_k) \setminus (L_0 \cup \dots \cup L_k),
  \]
  where $N^+(L)$ denotes the set of out-neighbours of the vertices of $L$. The set of
  vertices \emph{visited} within $k$ rounds is $V_k = L_0 \cup \dots \cup L_k$. When
  $s \notin \V{G}$ every layer is empty.
  In Lean the search is a state $(V_k, L_k)$ iterated $k$ times from $(\{s\}, \{s\})$,
  so that the definition reduces and \texttt{decide} can evaluate it.
nodes.clean_text: Let s in VG. The layers of breadth-first search from s are the sets \[ L_0 = \s\, L_k+1 = N^+(L_k) setminus (L_0 cup dots cup L_k), \] where N^+(L) denotes the set of out-neighbours of the vertices of L. The set of vertices visited within k rounds is V_k = L_0 cup dots cup L_k. When s notin VG every layer is empty. In Lean the search is a state (V_k, L_k) iterated k times from (\s\, \s\), so that the definition reduces and decide can evaluate it.
nodes.label: def:bfs-layers

nodes.name: Soundness
nodes.statement: Every vertex of L_k is the endpoint of a walk of length k from s.
conclusions: Every vertex of L_k is the endpoint of a walk of length k from s.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:bfs-sound}
  
  
  
  Every vertex of $L_k$ is the endpoint of a walk of length $k$ from $s$.
nodes.clean_text: Every vertex of L_k is the endpoint of a walk of length k from s.
nodes.label: lem:bfs-sound

nodes.statement: By induction on k: a vertex of L_k+1 is an out-neighbour of a vertex of L_k, and appending that arc to the walk given by the induction hypothesis yields a walk of length k + 1.
nodes.raw_latex:
By induction on $k$: a vertex of $L_{k+1}$ is an out-neighbour of a vertex of $L_k$,
  and appending that arc to the walk given by the induction hypothesis yields a walk of
  length $k + 1$.
nodes.clean_text: By induction on k: a vertex of L_k+1 is an out-neighbour of a vertex of L_k, and appending that arc to the walk given by the induction hypothesis yields a walk of length k + 1.

nodes.name: Completeness
nodes.statement: The endpoint of a walk of length ell from s lies in V_ell.
conclusions: The endpoint of a walk of length ell from s lies in V_ell.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem:bfs-complete}
  
  
  
  The endpoint of a walk of length $\ell$ from $s$ lies in $V_\ell$.
nodes.clean_text: The endpoint of a walk of length ell from s lies in V_ell.
nodes.label: lem:bfs-complete

nodes.statement: By induction on the walk. The key step is that the out-neighbours of a vertex of V_k lie in V_k+1: such a vertex lies in some L_j with j le k, and its out-neighbours are either already in V_j or in L_j+1.
nodes.raw_latex:
By induction on the walk. The key step is that the out-neighbours of a vertex of $V_k$
  lie in $V_{k+1}$: such a vertex lies in some $L_j$ with $j \le k$, and its
  out-neighbours are either already in $V_j$ or in $L_{j+1}$.

nodes.name: Termination
nodes.statement: If L_k neq emptyset then k < |VG|. Hence the search from s has exhausted every layer after |VG| rounds.
conclusions: Hence the search from s has exhausted every layer after |VG| rounds.
nodes.clean_text: If L_k neq emptyset then k < |VG|. Hence the search from s has exhausted every layer after |VG| rounds.
nodes.label: lem:bfs-termination

nodes.statement: An empty layer is followed by an empty layer, so L_0, dots, L_k are all non-empty. They are pairwise disjoint subsets of VG, so k + 1 le |V_k| le |VG|.
nodes.raw_latex:
An empty layer is followed by an empty layer, so $L_0, \dots, L_k$ are all non-empty.
  They are pairwise disjoint subsets of $\V{G}$, so $k + 1 \le |V_k| \le |\V{G}|$.

nodes.name: The layers are the spheres
nodes.statement: For every vertex v and every k in N, \[ v in L_k iff dist(s, v) = k . \]
assumptions: For every vertex v and every k in N
conclusions: \[ v in L_k iff dist(s, v) = k .

\label{thm:bfs-layers-spheres}
  
  
  
  For every vertex $v$ and every $k \in \N$,
  \[
    v \in L_k \iff \dist(s, v) = k .
  \]

nodes.statement: Let v in L_k. Soundness gives dist(s, v) le k. For the reverse inequality there is nothing to show when k = 0; when k = j + 1, a walk from s to v of length at most j would place v in V_j by completeness, whereas L_j+1 avoids V_j by construction, so dist(s, v) > j, i.e. dist(s, v) ge k. Conversely, if dist(s, v) = k then a shortest walk places v in V_k, so v in L_j for some j le k, and the first part gives j = k.
nodes.raw_latex:
Let $v \in L_k$. Soundness gives $\dist(s, v) \le k$. For the reverse inequality there
  is nothing to show when $k = 0$; when $k = j + 1$, a walk from $s$ to $v$ of length at
  most $j$ would place $v$ in $V_j$ by completeness, whereas $L_{j+1}$ avoids $V_j$ by
  construction, so $\dist(s, v) > j$, i.e. $\dist(s, v) \ge k$. Conversely, if
  $\dist(s, v) = k$ then a shortest walk places $v \in V_k$, so $v \in L_j$ for some
  $j \le k$, and the first part gives $j = k$.

Conversely, if dist(s, v) = k then a shortest walk places v in V_k, so v in L_j for some j le k, and the first part gives j = k.
